target_model_responses.dim2_response:
Below is a **hands‑on, step‑by‑step workflow** you can follow at home to **inspect, rework, and verify** a small electronic board. It assumes you are already comfortable with soldering and tracing circuits, and it pulls together the practical tool suggestions from our **glove‑friendly hand‑tool kit** [[summaries/session-39_2025-02-10]] and the **power‑path troubleshooting method** we discussed earlier [[summaries/session-06_2024-06-12]]. --- ## 1. Gather the “home‑lab” toolbox | Category | Suggested items (short description) | Why it matters | |----------|--------------------------------------|----------------| | **Power & measurement** | • Bench (adjustable) power supply with current‑limit (e.g., 0‑30 V, 0‑5 A)
• Digital multimeter (DMM) with diode/continuity mode
• Optional: 2‑channel oscilloscope (for regulator signatures) | Supplies controlled voltage, lets you verify rail levels, and catches shorts safely [[concepts/bench_supply_short_detection]]. | | **Soldering & rework** | • 60 W soldering iron with fine‑point tip
• Solder wick & brass desoldering braid
• Flux pen or paste
• Small tweezers, needle‑nose pliers
• Precision screwdriver set (including stubby ratcheting driver) | Enables clean removal and replacement of components without damaging pads. | | **Inspection & handling** | • Magnifying lamp or 10‑15× handheld magnifier
• Soft‑face hammer / magnetic pickup wand (for stray screws)
• Pocket caliper (measure component leads, pad spacing)
• Magnetic bit holder / wristband (keeps tools visible) | Improves visual feedback, especially when you’re wearing gloves or have limited tactile feel. | | **Safety** | • Anti‑static wrist strap
• Small discharge tool (resistor = 1 kΩ, 5 W) for capacitors
• Insulated tweezers | Prevents ESD damage and protects you from hidden charge. | --- ## 2. Safety‑first preparation 1. **Power‑off & unplug** the device. 2. **Discharge** any large electrolytic capacitors with the 1 kΩ discharge tool (hold for ~5 s). 3. **Ground yourself** with the anti‑static strap. 4. **Clear workspace** – lay down a static‑dissipative mat, keep screws and tiny parts in a magnetic tray. --- ## 3. Visual & photographic inspection 1. **Take a wide‑shot** of the board (USB‑C connector, power‑IC area, major inductors). 2. **Zoom in** on suspicious spots: cracked solder joints, burnt pads, missing components, or corrosion. 3. **Label the photo** (or sketch) with the **power‑tree stages** we discussed – input protection, charging controller, primary buck/boost, secondary LDOs [[concepts/power_path_troubleshooting]]. *Having a photo map makes the later probing steps faster (see the “photo‑based board analysis” concept).* --- ## 4. Initial continuity / resistance check (board un‑powered) | Action | DMM setting | How‑to | |--------|-------------|--------| | **Check for shorts to ground** on the USB‑C VBUS line | Diode/Continuity (beep) | Place one probe on the VBUS pin, the other on any ground point. A beep indicates a short. | | **Validate trace continuity** between key nodes | Ohms (Ω) | Probe from the input connector to the protection MOSFET drain, then to the charging‑IC VIN, etc. Expect low (< 10 Ω) resistance for copper traces. | | **Identify open solder joints** | Resistance (high Ω) | A very high reading where you expect continuity signals a cracked joint. | If you spot a short, **isolate it** (e.g., desolder the nearest suspect component, re‑measure). This mirrors the **bench‑supply short‑detection** technique [[concepts/bench_supply_short_detection]]. --- ## 5. Targeted rework 1. **Apply flux** to the suspect joint. 2. **Heat the pad and lead** with the soldering iron; gently **pull the lead** with tweezers to lift it off. 3. **Clean** the pad with solder wick and a little fresh solder. 4. **Re‑place** the component (or a replacement) and **tack‑solder** it, then **reflow** a proper fillet. 5. **Inspect** under magnification for solder bridges or cold joints. *For tiny surface‑mount parts (e.g., MOSFETs, inductors), a fine‑point tip and a small amount of flux make the job much cleaner.* --- ## 6. Power‑up safety test with bench supply 1. **Set the supply** to **+5 V** (or the nominal input of the board) with **current limit at 200 mA**. 2. **Connect** the supply to the board’s **input power pins** (USB‑C VBUS pins or barrel‑jack). 3. **Observe** the current readout: * If current spikes > 200 mA instantly, a short is still present – lower the limit further and investigate. * If current stays low, proceed to the next step. This staged approach lets you locate shorts without damaging components, as described in the **bench‑supply short‑detection** concept. --- ## 7. Verify each power stage | Stage | Expected voltage (typical) | Probe points | What to look for | |-------|----------------------------|--------------|------------------| | **Input protection** | ~5 V (raw) | Input pin → after reverse‑polarity diode/MOSFET | ~5 V present, small diode drop (0.3‑0.6 V). | | **Charging controller / Power‑path IC** | 4.2 V (battery voltage) | IC VIN, VBAT pins | Battery voltage appears, no excessive drop. | | **Primary buck/boost** | 3.3 V (or as per board) | Output rail (e.g., VCC) | Stable 3.3 V, low ripple (< 20 mV). | | **Secondary LDOs** | 1.8 V, 1.2 V, etc. | Individual regulator outputs | Correct levels, smooth DC. | Use the **multimeter voltage mode** for each node. If you have an oscilloscope, **capture the switching waveform** on the buck/boost node: a regular PWM train indicates the regulator is enabled; a flat line suggests it’s disabled or dead [[concepts/buck_regulator_scope_signatures]]. --- ## 8. Functional test 1. **Power the board** with the normal USB‑C charger (now you know the internal rails are good). 2. **Check LEDs, display, or other indicators** to confirm the device “boots”. 3. **Run a quick load test** (e.g., press a button that draws a few mA) and verify that voltage remains stable. If the board still doesn’t work, repeat steps 4‑7 focusing on the stage that failed to reach its expected voltage. --- ## 9. Documentation & clean‑up * **Take a final photo** of the repaired board and note any component replacements. * **Store** the used screws and tiny parts in the magnetic tray for the next job. * **Update** your personal repair log (date, board type, steps taken, outcome). --- ### Quick reference checklist (print & stick on your bench) 1. ☐ Safety – unplug, discharge, ESD strap 2. ☐ Photos & power‑tree sketch 3. ☐ DMM continuity / resistance sweep 4. ☐ Identify & re‑work bad joints (flux → desolder → clean → re‑solder) 5. ☐ Bench‑supply power‑up with current limit 6. ☐ Verify each rail (measure voltages) 7. ☐ Optional oscilloscope: look for PWM on buck/boost 8. ☐ Full functional test with original charger 9. ☐ Document & tidy workspace --- By following this ordered plan—**visual inspection → continuity check → targeted rework → safe power‑up → stage‑by‑stage verification**—you’ll be able to diagnose, fix, and confirm operation of a small board using only the common tools we listed. Happy soldering!
